desc:
There are 3m piles of coins; piles[i] is the number of coins in pile i. You play with two friends, Alice and Bob, until no pile is left. In every round:

  • you pick any three of the remaining piles,
  • Alice takes the pile with the most coins of the three,
  • you take the pile with the second most coins (with ties, any order gives the same pile size),
  • Bob takes the remaining, smallest pile.

Return the maximum total number of coins you can collect.

piles = [2, 4, 1, 2, 7, 8]            -> 9   (round 1: 2,7,8 you take 7; round 2: 1,2,4 you take 2)
piles = [2, 4, 5]                     -> 4
piles = [9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4]   -> 18
constraints: 3 ≤ piles.length ≤ 9,999 and piles.length is a multiple of 3
hints: Alice always gets the largest of the three. What is the best way to make her waste as little as possible?
Bob's pile is wasted too. Give Bob the smallest piles in the whole input.
Sort. Bob takes the smallest m piles. Among the remaining 2m piles, pair them from the top: you take the 2nd, 4th, 6th ... largest piles overall.
editorial: You choose the triples, so choose them to feed Alice and Bob as little as possible. In every round the largest pile of the triple is lost to Alice, so the best we can do is let her take the next biggest piles and put ourselves right below her: take the two largest remaining piles together with the smallest remaining pile as the triple. Alice gets the largest, you get the second largest, Bob is stuck with the smallest.

After sorting ascending, Bob receives the first m = n / 3 piles and you collect the piles at sorted positions n-2, n-4, ..., n/3 (m piles in total). Swapping any other arrangement into this one never decreases your total, because the smallest piles are the least useful to anyone else. Sorting dominates: O(n log n).
solution:
def maxCoins(piles):
    piles = sorted(piles)
    n = len(piles)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n // 3, n, 2):
        total += piles[i]
    return total
